# Use Writing Blocks with ChatGPT for Teachers

So when you ask Chat to create something, you probably want to revise or reuse, think like a letter to families or a lesson plan, an update to the staff in my school, a handout that I'm going to give my students. What's great is ChatGPT can place that draft in an editable writing block directly in the conversation. So for this example, I'm going to ask Chat to create a family-facing handout about school attendance, and I'll include a very clear instruction at the end saying, "I want you to place this draft in a writing block." So if we go into Chat, we are going to drag and drop a PDF. This is a school policy, so this is just a super technical policy that lives on our website. I've downloaded it as a PDF. Alternatively, I could just give it the link to that website, and I'm going to add this prompt along with it. I'm going to say, "Draft a one-page family-friendly handout explaining what our attached school attendance policy typically means, why regular attendance matters, et cetera." I could say, "Put this in a writing block to make sure that the writing block product is used" but we're actually going to leave it out and see if it does it anyway. So we're going to press send here. It's going to look through this file. It's going to start to respond to my request, and we'll give it a moment. So I can see it's starting to write this. I can click directly in here once this finishes and edit the text myself. I don't need to send a new prompt or any small wording change. So what I can do is just click and start adding. So I can interact with this just like I would a document. But what's very cool is I can also use AI to start to transform different pieces of this. So I'm going to select this first paragraph. I'll just highlight it, and I'm going to ask for some changes. Let's say, "Make this tone warmer and more welcoming." And then it'll suggest something. It'll think for a moment, suggest something. If I like it, I can accept it, and again, really cool way to interact with this. What's great is this can also translate, so I could say, "Translate this document to Mandarin." Since I know that students in my course have, although they speak English, some of their family doesn't, I can create really accessible documents that are available to non-English speakers as well and include this maybe at the bottom or as a separate version that I share. Of all of the translation products out there, I've found Chat to be the best. What's great is it'll look at a sentence or a paragraph in its entirety and make sure that it's capturing the context of that sentence or paragraph as it translates, rather than just translating one specific word one at a time, which sometimes can make things sound a little funky.
